cards.says: Fruit and seed. What is your seed wearing, and what is it for?

segments.text: What is your seed wearing, and what is it for?

cards.says: What it is for. Find the fruits and seeds our grounds are giving away this month, and work out what every seed carries: a plant, a packed lunch, a coat, and a way of travelling. The skill is looking and touching.

segments.text: Find the fruits and seeds our grounds are giving away this month, and work out what every seed carries: a plant, a packed lunch, a coat, and a way of travelling.
The skill is looking and touching.

cards.says: The idea to carry. Children gather the fruits and seeds their grounds are letting go this month, look closely at what each one is wearing, drop them to see how they travel, and work out what every seed carries: a plant, a packed lunch, a coat, and a way of travelling.

segments.text: Children gather the fruits and seeds their grounds are letting go this month, look closely at what each one is wearing, drop them to see how they travel, and work out what every seed carries: a plant, a packed lunch, a coat, and a way of travelling.

cards.says: Why it matters. Autumn is the one month of the year when a whole plant's plan is lying on the ground where a five-year-old can pick it up.

segments.text: Autumn is the one month of the year when a whole plant's plan is lying on the ground where a five-year-old can pick it up.

cards.says: Before you go out. Two things to gather. Walk your hedge or your trees the day before and see what is down. If nothing has fallen yet, a bag of conkers, acorns or sycamore keys from a park does the same job.

cards.says: How it runs. You start with Find. Set the boundary first: this hedge, this tree, this patch of ground. Pairs work well, one tray between them.

segments.text: Set the boundary first: this hedge, this tree, this patch of ground.
Pairs work well, one tray between them.

cards.says: Then Look. Everything on the tray is wearing something: a wing, a cup, a shell, a skin, a hook. The wearing is the whole lesson.

segments.text: Everything on the tray is wearing something: a wing, a cup, a shell, a skin, a hook.
The wearing is the whole lesson.

cards.says: Then Travel. Hold a sycamore key up high and let it go, then a conker. The class sees the difference before anyone explains it.

segments.text: Hold a sycamore key up high and let it go, then a conker.

cards.says: Then What a seed carries. Four things they can look for in anything they pick up. Try them on an acorn, a sycamore key, a conker, a blackberry.

segments.text: Four things they can look for in anything they pick up.
Try them on an acorn, a sycamore key, a conker, a blackberry.

cards.says: And finish in Circle. Let them argue it out. The wings usually win, but a berry a bird carries goes further than any of them. Any guess counts as thinking like a scientist. No right answer.

cards.says: Why leaves turn. Where does the green go?
What it is for. Find out why leaves change colour and fall: the tree is taking its green back in before winter, and the other colours were there all along. The skill is looking closely.

segments.text: Find out why leaves change colour and fall: the tree is taking its green back in before winter, and the other colours were there all along.

cards.says: The idea to carry. Children walk under the turning trees, bring back one fallen leaf each, lay them out from greenest to brownest, and work out that the tree is taking its green back in before winter and the other colours were there all along.

segments.text: Children walk under the turning trees, bring back one fallen leaf each, lay them out from greenest to brownest, and work out that the tree is taking its green back in before winter and the other colours were there all along.

cards.says: Why it matters. Every child has been told that leaves change colour in autumn; almost none have been told why, and the real reason is simple enough for a five-year-old.

segments.text: Every child has been told that leaves change colour in autumn; almost none have been told why, and the real reason is simple enough for a five-year-old.

cards.says: Before you go out. Nothing to bring.
How it runs. You start with Walk. One leaf each, from the ground, chosen for its colour. Ask them not to pull leaves off a branch: those have not finished yet.

segments.text: One leaf each, from the ground, chosen for its colour.

cards.says: Then The colour line. Lay every leaf on the ground in one long line, greenest at one end, brownest at the other. Let the class argue about where each one goes.

cards.says: Then Why. The green is the tree's food-maker and it is expensive. Before winter the tree takes it back inside and stores it. The yellows and oranges were in the leaf the whole time, hidden underneath.

cards.says: Then Letting go. Find the stalk end. There is a small clean scar where the leaf joined the branch. The tree built that. It let go on purpose.

cards.says: And finish in Circle. Let a few children hold theirs up for the whole circle. Back into the tree, kept until spring. Say it plainly. It is a good, true answer. No right answer. Ice, wind, weight, the dark. Big guesses welcome.

cards.says: Where the leaves go. Why is our playground not buried in leaves?

segments.text: Why is our playground not buried in leaves?

cards.says: What it is for. Find out what happens to all the fallen leaves: they are eaten, and they become the soil the next plants grow in. The skill is looking and touching.

segments.text: Find out what happens to all the fallen leaves: they are eaten, and they become the soil the next plants grow in.
The skill is looking and touching.

cards.says: The idea to carry. Children lift the fallen leaves to meet the woodlice, worms and fungus threads eating them, dig down to the layer where leaves stop looking like leaves, and find that it has become soil.

segments.text: Children lift the fallen leaves to meet the woodlice, worms and fungus threads eating them, dig down to the layer where leaves stop looking like leaves, and find that it has become soil.

cards.says: Why it matters. The question this session opens with, why is the playground not buried in leaves, has an answer a child can hold in their hand. Nothing here is thrown away: it is eaten, and it becomes the next thing.

segments.text: The question this session opens with, why is the playground not buried in leaves, has an answer a child can hold in their hand.

cards.says: Before you go out. Three things to gather. Bring the bug pots, the magnifying glasses and hand wipes for afterwards. Find your leaf pile the day before: a corner where leaves gather, a hedge bottom, a log. Check it for anything sharp.

segments.text: Bring the bug pots, the magnifying glasses and hand wipes for afterwards.

cards.says: Then Lift. Lift, look, and put back exactly as you found it. Two hands under a log, rolled towards them so nothing runs over their fingers.

cards.says: Then Crumble. This is the moment of the lesson. Dig down to where the leaves have stopped looking like leaves. Rub it between finger and thumb: dark, damp, crumbly, and it used to be a tree.

cards.says: And finish in Circle. We borrow, we look, we give back. The whole lesson in one move. Woodlice, worms, slugs, and the fungus threads. Any guess counts as thinking like a scientist. No right answer. Everything that ever fell here, all the way down.

cards.says: Getting ready for winter. Who is getting ready for the cold?

segments.text: Who is getting ready for the cold?

cards.says: What it is for. Notice that the light is going and the year is turning, and find the four answers the living things around us give to winter: store it, sleep through it, leave, or die back and wait underground. The skill is looking and wondering.

segments.text: Notice that the light is going and the year is turning, and find the four answers the living things around us give to winter: store it, sleep through it, leave, or die back and wait underground.
The skill is looking and wondering.

cards.says: The idea to carry. Children mark where their own shadow ends, hunt for the evidence of animals and plants preparing for the cold, and sort what they find into the four answers to winter: store it, sleep through it, leave, or die back and wait underground.

segments.text: Children mark where their own shadow ends, hunt for the evidence of animals and plants preparing for the cold, and sort what they find into the four answers to winter: store it, sleep through it, leave, or die back and wait underground.

cards.says: Why it matters. Autumn is a countdown a child can watch happening.

segments.text: Autumn is a countdown a child can watch happening.

cards.says: Before you go out. One thing to gather. Bring a stone per pair, or chalk if your ground is hard. Go out at the time of day you could come back at, so the shadows can be put side by side later. Nothing else.

segments.text: Bring a stone per pair, or chalk if your ground is hard.
Go out at the time of day you could come back at, so the shadows can be put side by side later.

cards.says: How it runs. You start with Shadow. This one needs sun. If the sky is flat grey, say so honestly, go straight to the hunt, and mark the shadows on the first bright day instead.

segments.text: If the sky is flat grey, say so honestly, go straight to the hunt, and mark the shadows on the first bright day instead.

cards.says: Then Hunt. Nibbled nuts, empty shells, a hole at the bottom of a hedge, a web, a nest showing now the leaves are thinning, a bush stripped of its berries. Evidence, not animals.

segments.text: Nibbled nuts, empty shells, a hole at the bottom of a hedge, a web, a nest showing now the leaves are thinning, a bush stripped of its berries.

cards.says: Then Four answers. Four answers they can hold anything against. Try them on a squirrel, a hedgehog, a swallow, a daffodil.

segments.text: Four answers they can hold anything against.
Try them on a squirrel, a hedgehog, a swallow, a daffodil.

cards.says: Then Us. Same problem, same four answers. Coats and a full cupboard are storing. The lights going on earlier is the light going. Let them find the parallels.

segments.text: Coats and a full cupboard are storing.
The lights going on earlier is the light going.

cards.says: And finish in Circle. Let a few children hold their evidence up for the whole circle. Hedgehogs, bats, some butterflies behind the shed. Any guess counts as thinking like a scientist. No right answer. Longer, until midwinter, and then it starts coming back. Big guesses welcome.

segments.text: Let a few children hold their evidence up for the whole circle.

cards.says: Autumn detectives. How do we know autumn has arrived?

segments.text: How do we know autumn has arrived?

cards.says: What it is for. Notice and name the changes autumn has made to the garden, using all the senses. The skill is noticing change.

segments.text: Notice and name the changes autumn has made to the garden, using all the senses.

cards.says: The idea to carry. Autumn is the most visible season: leaves turn and fall, air cools, rain and wind pick up, plants die back and animals change what they do. This first session does not teach any of that.

segments.text: Autumn is the most visible season: leaves turn and fall, air cools, rain and wind pick up, plants die back and animals change what they do.

cards.says: Why it matters. A child who is told it is autumn learns a word. A child who finds autumn, in a colder railing or a yellowing leaf, learns that looking works. That confidence is the foundation for every investigation that follows.

cards.says: Before you go out. Three things to gather. Walk the space yourself the day before and find three changes worth being led to: a tree turning, a patch of fallen leaves, a plant dying back. You will not point them out; you will steer the wander past them.

segments.text: Walk the space yourself the day before and find three changes worth being led to: a tree turning, a patch of fallen leaves, a plant dying back.

cards.says: How it runs. You start with Settle. Give this longer than feels comfortable. A class goes quiet on its own once it is hunting for a sound, and the quiet you wait for lasts longer than the quiet you ask for. Say this one clearly.

segments.text: Give this longer than feels comfortable.
A class goes quiet on its own once it is hunting for a sound, and the quiet you wait for lasts longer than the quiet you ask for.

cards.says: Then The detective brief. Resist naming autumn yourself. The word should arrive from a child, or wait. The mystery frame only works while the answer is theirs to find.

cards.says: Then The evidence hunt. Steer the wander past the three changes you scouted, without pointing. Kneel beside whoever finds one and ask what they think happened here. The question does more than the answer.

cards.says: Earth, air and water. What is changing the garden: earth, air or water?

segments.text: What is changing the garden: earth, air or water?

cards.says: What it is for. Investigate how soil, wind and water are each changing the garden, and find autumn's warm colours. The skill is investigating.

segments.text: Investigate how soil, wind and water are each changing the garden, and find autumn's warm colours.

cards.says: The idea to carry. Three short investigations in one session: earth, air and water, each met with hands and senses rather than words.

cards.says: From leaf to soil. Where does a fallen leaf go?

cards.says: Falling. What here is letting go?

What it is for. Autumn is the season of letting go. Children find things that are falling (leaves, seeds, petals) and hold the moment of release. A practice about endings and transformation. The skill is looking and touching.

segments.text: Autumn is the season of letting go. Children find things that are falling (leaves, seeds, petals) and hold the moment of release. A practice about endings and transformation.
The skill is looking and touching.

cards.says: The idea to carry. Autumn is the season of letting go. Deciduous trees stop feeding their leaves, the leaves change colour and loosen, and one by one they fall.

segments.text: Autumn is the season of letting go.
Deciduous trees stop feeding their leaves, the leaves change colour and loosen, and one by one they fall.

cards.says: Why it matters. Falling leaves give young children a gentle, visible way to meet the idea of endings. Nothing is lost here: a fallen leaf is on its way to becoming soil that feeds next year's growth.

segments.text: Falling leaves give young children a gentle, visible way to meet the idea of endings.
Nothing is lost here: a fallen leaf is on its way to becoming soil that feeds next year's growth.

cards.says: Before you go out. One thing to gather. Best when leaves are actively falling. Any area with deciduous trees works.

segments.text: Best when leaves are actively falling.
Any area with deciduous trees works.

cards.says: How it runs. You start with Find something falling. Autumn is the season of release. Let them find their own examples. Don't direct too much.

segments.text: You start with Find something falling.
Autumn is the season of release.
Let them find their own examples.

cards.says: Then Catch one. A fallen leaf was connected to a tree for months. Now it's free. Feel the weight of that lightness.

segments.text: A fallen leaf was connected to a tree for months.
Feel the weight of that lightness.

cards.says: Then Wonder. This is deep for younger kids. Keep it light. Older KS2 can handle the depth. Follow their lead.

segments.text: This is deep for younger kids.
Older KS2 can handle the depth.

cards.says: Then Send it on. The leaf will become soil. That's not an ending. Walk back.
And finish in Circle. Share findings. Decomposition, soil, new life. The cycle. Optional. For reflective classes only.

cards.says: Soil. What is the ground made of?

segments.text: What is the ground made of?

cards.says: What it is for. A return to the ground. Children pick up handfuls of soil, smell it, squeeze it, and discover that everything that ever lived here is now part of the earth beneath their feet. The skill is touching and smelling.

segments.text: A return to the ground. Children pick up handfuls of soil, smell it, squeeze it, and discover that everything that ever lived here is now part of the earth beneath their feet.
The skill is touching and smelling.

cards.says: The idea to carry. Soil is not just dirt. It is a whole world made of broken-down leaves, tiny stones, sand, clay, roots and small living things, all mixed together.

segments.text: It is a whole world made of broken-down leaves, tiny stones, sand, clay, roots and small living things, all mixed together.

cards.says: Why it matters. Children walk on soil every day without ever really meeting it.

segments.text: Children walk on soil every day without ever really meeting it.

cards.says: Before you go out. One thing to gather. Find an area with accessible soil. A garden bed or base of a tree works well.

segments.text: Find an area with accessible soil.
A garden bed or base of a tree works well.

cards.says: How it runs. You start with Look at the soil. Not just "dirt." Leaves, twigs, stones, sand, clay, roots, insects. It's a whole world.

segments.text: You start with Look at the soil.
Leaves, twigs, stones, sand, clay, roots, insects.

cards.says: Then Hold the soil. Crumbly, damp, gritty, smooth. Each type of soil tells a story about what lives in it.

segments.text: Each type of soil tells a story about what lives in it.

cards.says: Then Wonder. Decomposition as transformation. The leaf became the soil the seed grows in.

segments.text: The leaf became the soil the seed grows in.

cards.says: Then Put it back. Same closing as Spring's Underground practice. The earth holds us. Walk back.

segments.text: Same closing as Spring's Underground practice.

cards.says: And finish in Circle. Compare different spots: some sandy, some clay, some leafy. Earthy, musty, damp, alive. Build vocabulary. Connects to food, life, everything.

cards.says: Colours. Which colours are leaving, and which are arriving?

segments.text: Which colours are leaving, and which are arriving?

cards.says: What it is for. The autumn colour change in real time. Children find leaves halfway between green and gold, catalogue the arriving and departing colours, and witness transformation happening slowly. The skill is noticing by looking.

segments.text: The autumn colour change in real time. Children find leaves halfway between green and gold, catalogue the arriving and departing colours, and witness transformation happening slowly.
The skill is noticing by looking.

cards.says: The idea to carry. In autumn, deciduous trees stop making the green that fills their leaves all summer. As the green fades, the yellows, oranges, reds and browns that were hidden underneath begin to show.

segments.text: In autumn, deciduous trees stop making the green that fills their leaves all summer.
As the green fades, the yellows, oranges, reds and browns that were hidden underneath begin to show.

cards.says: Why it matters. The autumn colour change is one of the most beautiful slow things a child can watch, and it is happening on a schedule no one controls.

segments.text: The autumn colour change is one of the most beautiful slow things a child can watch, and it is happening on a schedule no one controls.

cards.says: Before you go out. One thing to gather. Best during peak autumn colour (October). Any area with deciduous trees.
How it runs. You start with Watch the colours turn. Green is leaving. Yellow, orange, red, brown are arriving. Let them catalogue the transition.

segments.text: You start with Watch the colours turn.
Yellow, orange, red, brown are arriving.

cards.says: Then Find the turning leaf. A half-turned leaf is autumn captured. Two colours on one surface.

segments.text: A half-turned leaf is autumn captured.

cards.says: Then Wonder. Patience and presence. Autumn teaches slowness.
Then Thank the colours. Autumn colour is brief and brilliant. Gratitude for impermanence.

segments.text: Autumn colour is brief and brilliant.

cards.says: And finish in Circle. Greens fading. Gold, amber, crimson, brown. Science connection: chlorophyll, sugars, light.

cards.says: Quiet. What is the quietest sound you can hear?

segments.text: What is the quietest sound you can hear?

cards.says: What it is for. The soundscape narrows. Children listen for what's missing (fewer birds, fewer insects) and discover that in the quiet, deeper sounds emerge. The skill is noticing by listening.

segments.text: The soundscape narrows. Children listen for what's missing (fewer birds, fewer insects) and discover that in the quiet, deeper sounds emerge.
The skill is noticing by listening.

cards.says: The idea to carry. As autumn deepens, the soundscape thins out. Many birds have stopped their spring song, insects have gone quiet, and the busy hum of summer fades.

segments.text: As autumn deepens, the soundscape thins out.
Many birds have stopped their spring song, insects have gone quiet, and the busy hum of summer fades.

cards.says: Why it matters. Learning to be still and really listen is a skill children rarely get to practise, and autumn gives the perfect conditions: a quieter world where subtle sounds can finally be heard.

segments.text: Learning to be still and really listen is a skill children rarely get to practise, and autumn gives the perfect conditions: a quieter world where subtle sounds can finally be heard.

cards.says: Before you go out. One thing to gather. Choose a time when the school is quieter (not during break time). The contrast matters.

segments.text: Choose a time when the school is quieter (not during break time).

cards.says: How it runs. You start with Notice what's missing. Fewer birds singing. Fewer insects buzzing. The soundscape of autumn is quieter than summer.

segments.text: You start with Notice what's missing.
The soundscape of autumn is quieter than summer.

cards.says: Then Listen. Wind in branches, a robin, distant traffic, crunching leaves underfoot. The autumn orchestra is smaller but still playing.

segments.text: Wind in branches, a robin, distant traffic, crunching leaves underfoot.
The autumn orchestra is smaller but still playing.

cards.says: Then Wonder. Subtle sounds emerge in silence. Your own breathing. A faraway bird. Water somewhere.
Then Thank the quiet. Walk back in silence. See how long the class can hold it.

segments.text: See how long the class can hold it.

cards.says: And finish in Circle. The most subtle observation wins. Bees, lawn mowers, birdsong. Where did they go? Personal preference. No right answer.

cards.says: Bulbs. What is being stored away for next year?

segments.text: What is being stored away for next year?

cards.says: What it is for. Autumn is when things get buried for later. Children find seeds, nuts, and berries being stored and reflect on the idea of resting before growing. The skill is touching and looking.

segments.text: Autumn is when things get buried for later. Children find seeds, nuts, and berries being stored and reflect on the idea of resting before growing.
The skill is touching and looking.

cards.says: The idea to carry. Autumn is when nature banks for the future. Trees drop seeds, nuts and berries, squirrels bury acorns, seeds work their way into cracks in the ground, and bulbs sit waiting underground.

segments.text: Autumn is when nature banks for the future.
Trees drop seeds, nuts and berries, squirrels bury acorns, seeds work their way into cracks in the ground, and bulbs sit waiting underground.

cards.says: Why it matters. The idea that something can look finished, a fallen acorn, a dropped berry, yet hold a whole new plant or a whole next spring inside it, is a quietly powerful one for young children.

segments.text: The idea that something can look finished, a fallen acorn, a dropped berry, yet hold a whole new plant or a whole next spring inside it, is a quietly powerful one for young children.

cards.says: Before you go out. One thing to gather. Best in areas where nuts, seeds, or berries can be found on the ground.

segments.text: Best in areas where nuts, seeds, or berries can be found on the ground.

cards.says: How it runs. You start with Find what's stored away. Squirrels burying nuts, seeds falling into cracks, berries dropping. Nature is banking for the future.

segments.text: You start with Find what's stored away.
Squirrels burying nuts, seeds falling into cracks, berries dropping.
Nature is banking for the future.

cards.says: Then Hold the promise. An acorn, a conker, a rosehip. Each one contains next spring.

segments.text: An acorn, a conker, a rosehip.

cards.says: Then Wonder. Seasonal metaphor for inner life. Light touch. Optional for younger groups.
Then Tuck it in. Push an acorn into soft earth. Walk back.

segments.text: Push an acorn into soft earth.

cards.says: And finish in Circle. Seeds, nuts, berries: nature's savings account. Preparation, survival, planning ahead. Knowledge, friendships, memories. Metaphor territory.

segments.text: Seeds, nuts, berries: nature's savings account.

cards.says: The last warmth. Where can you still find warmth?

segments.text: Where can you still find warmth?

cards.says: What it is for. The closing practice of autumn. Children search for the last warm spots before winter arrives (sun-warmed surfaces, sheltered corners) and say goodbye to the warmth. The skill is noticing by touching.

segments.text: The closing practice of autumn. Children search for the last warm spots before winter arrives (sun-warmed surfaces, sheltered corners) and say goodbye to the warmth.
The skill is noticing by touching.

cards.says: The idea to carry. This is the closing practice of autumn. Winter is coming, and the warmth is retreating: fewer warm days, cooler ground, less sun.

segments.text: This is the closing practice of autumn.
Winter is coming, and the warmth is retreating: fewer warm days, cooler ground, less sun.

cards.says: Why it matters. Ending autumn by seeking out its last warmth teaches children to treasure something exactly because it is fleeting, a gentle, hopeful lesson rather than a sad one.

segments.text: Ending autumn by seeking out its last warmth teaches children to treasure something exactly because it is fleeting, a gentle, hopeful lesson rather than a sad one.

cards.says: Before you go out. One thing to gather. Best on a cool autumn day when warmth is noticeable. Scout for sun-warmed surfaces.

segments.text: Best on a cool autumn day when warmth is noticeable.

cards.says: How it runs. You start with Find the last warmth. A sun-warmed bench, a sheltered corner, warm bark, their own hands in pockets. The warmth is retreating.

segments.text: You start with Find the last warmth.
A sun-warmed bench, a sheltered corner, warm bark, their own hands in pockets.

cards.says: Then Hold the warmth. Present-moment awareness. The warmth of autumn is finite and precious.

segments.text: The warmth of autumn is finite and precious.

cards.says: Then Wonder. The seasonal cycle as a comfort. Winter is not forever.

segments.text: The seasonal cycle as a comfort.

cards.says: Then Say see you. Close the autumn season. Walk back slowly.
And finish in Circle. Compare the last warm spots. Anticipation of winter. Not fear: curiosity. Close autumn with hope, not loss.

segments.text: Close autumn with hope, not loss.

cards.says: Bare. What can you see now the leaves are gone?

segments.text: What can you see now the leaves are gone?

cards.says: What it is for. Leaves are gone and the hidden structure of trees is revealed. Children see nests, branches, and sky that were invisible in summer. A practice about what becomes visible when things are stripped away. The skill is noticing by looking.

segments.text: Leaves are gone and the hidden structure of trees is revealed. Children see nests, branches, and sky that were invisible in summer. A practice about what becomes visible when things are stripped away.
The skill is noticing by looking.

cards.says: The idea to carry. In winter, deciduous trees drop their leaves and stand bare. Suddenly you can see the whole shape of a tree: the trunk, the branches splitting into smaller and smaller twigs, and the sky behind them.

segments.text: In winter, deciduous trees drop their leaves and stand bare.
Suddenly you can see the whole shape of a tree: the trunk, the branches splitting into smaller and smaller twigs, and the sky behind them.

cards.says: Why it matters. Children often think a bare tree is a dead tree. It isn't. It is resting, holding next year's leaves inside tiny buds.

segments.text: Children often think a bare tree is a dead tree.
It is resting, holding next year's leaves inside tiny buds.

cards.says: Before you go out. One thing to gather. Best after leaf fall when tree structures are fully visible.

segments.text: Best after leaf fall when tree structures are fully visible.

cards.says: How it runs. You start with Find what was hidden. Nests, branches, the shape of trunks, buildings behind trees, the sky itself. Winter reveals.

segments.text: You start with Find what was hidden.
Nests, branches, the shape of trunks, buildings behind trees, the sky itself.

cards.says: Then Trace a branch. The architecture of a tree. In summer it's hidden by leaves. Now you can see the whole structure.

segments.text: In summer it's hidden by leaves.
Now you can see the whole structure.

cards.says: Then Wonder. Dormancy is not death. The buds are already there, tiny and waiting. Point one out if you see one.

segments.text: The buds are already there, tiny and waiting.
Point one out if you see one.

cards.says: Then Thank the tree. Vulnerability as strength. Walk back.
And finish in Circle. Nests, structures, the sky. Drawing opportunity: sketch the branch pattern. Personal connection to dormancy.

segments.text: Drawing opportunity: sketch the branch pattern.

cards.says: Ice. What does frozen feel like?

What it is for. Water becomes something entirely different just from cold. Children find frozen things, touch ice, and reflect on transformation: how something can change completely and still be itself. The skill is touching and looking.

segments.text: Water becomes something entirely different just from cold. Children find frozen things, touch ice, and reflect on transformation: how something can change completely and still be itself.
The skill is touching and looking.

cards.says: The idea to carry. When the air gets cold enough, water freezes. A puddle turns to hard ice, dew on the grass becomes white frost, and mud sets solid.

segments.text: When the air gets cold enough, water freezes.
A puddle turns to hard ice, dew on the grass becomes white frost, and mud sets solid.

cards.says: Why it matters. Freezing is one of the first big changes a young child can see, touch and understand with their own hands. It shows that the same stuff can take different forms.

segments.text: Freezing is one of the first big changes a young child can see, touch and understand with their own hands.
It shows that the same stuff can take different forms.

cards.says: Before you go out. One thing to gather. Best on a frosty morning. If no frost, focus on the coldest surfaces and visible breath.

segments.text: If no frost, focus on the coldest surfaces and visible breath.

cards.says: How it runs. You start with Find something frozen. If there's no frost, look for cold: the coldest surface, condensation on metal, breath visible in air.

segments.text: You start with Find something frozen.
If there's no frost, look for cold: the coldest surface, condensation on metal, breath visible in air.

cards.says: Then Touch the ice. Sharp, smooth, brittle, stinging. Ice is water doing something extraordinary.

segments.text: Ice is water doing something extraordinary.

cards.says: Then Wonder. Transformation metaphor. Temperature changed water. What changes us?
Then Leave it to thaw. Continuity. Will it still be frozen tomorrow? Observation as care. Walk back.

segments.text: Will it still be frozen tomorrow?

cards.says: And finish in Circle. Puddles, leaves, grass, metal surfaces. It goes back to being water. Nothing is permanent. Optional. Transformation theme.

segments.text: It goes back to being water.

cards.says: Birds. Which birds stayed, and what are they doing?

segments.text: Which birds stayed, and what are they doing?

cards.says: What it is for. Most creatures left or hid. But the birds stayed. Children find a winter bird, watch it work, and reflect on what it means to stay when things are hard. The skill is looking and listening.

segments.text: Most creatures left or hid. But the birds stayed. Children find a winter bird, watch it work, and reflect on what it means to stay when things are hard.
The skill is looking and listening.

cards.says: The idea to carry. Many animals leave or hide away in winter, but some birds stay all season. They spend their short cold days working hard to find enough to eat: hopping across grass, searching hedges, pecking at the ground.

segments.text: Many animals leave or hide away in winter, but some birds stay all season.
They spend their short cold days working hard to find enough to eat: hopping across grass, searching hedges, pecking at the ground.

cards.says: Why it matters. Watching one bird do its work is a gateway to paying attention to everything. It builds patience and slow looking, which children get few chances to practise.

segments.text: Watching one bird do its work is a gateway to paying attention to everything.
It builds patience and slow looking, which children get few chances to practise.

cards.says: Before you go out. One thing to gather. Best in the morning when birds are most active feeding. Near feeders if your school has them.

segments.text: Best in the morning when birds are most active feeding.
Near feeders if your school has them.

cards.says: How it runs. You start with Find a bird. Robins, pigeons, crows, sparrows, blue tits. They're here all winter. That takes something.

segments.text: You start with Find a bird.
Robins, pigeons, crows, sparrows, blue tits.

cards.says: Then Watch a bird. Winter birds work hard. Every moment is about finding enough to eat. Observe for 2 minutes.

segments.text: Every moment is about finding enough to eat.

cards.says: Then Wonder. Resilience. Some kids will connect this to their own experiences. Let them.

segments.text: Some kids will connect this to their own experiences.

cards.says: Then Welcome it. Acknowledgment. The bird doesn't need our thanks, but saying it changes us. Walk back.

segments.text: The bird doesn't need our thanks, but saying it changes us.

cards.says: And finish in Circle. Build observation skills. Migration vs residency. Science connection. Beautiful question. Handle with care.

cards.says: Hibernation. Where might something be sleeping all winter?

segments.text: Where might something be sleeping all winter?

cards.says: What it is for. Somewhere nearby, creatures are sleeping through winter. Children look for likely hiding spots (under logs, in leaf piles, in wall cracks) without disturbing the sleepers. The skill is looking and touching.

segments.text: Somewhere nearby, creatures are sleeping through winter. Children look for likely hiding spots (under logs, in leaf piles, in wall cracks) without disturbing the sleepers.
The skill is looking and touching.

cards.says: The idea to carry. Some animals get through winter by sleeping through it. Hedgehogs, frogs, and many insects find a sheltered spot, slow their bodies right down, and stay hidden until spring.

segments.text: Some animals get through winter by sleeping through it.
Hedgehogs, frogs, and many insects find a sheltered spot, slow their bodies right down, and stay hidden until spring.

cards.says: Why it matters. Hibernation gives children a lovely, gentle idea: that rest is not laziness but survival, and that a sleeping creature deserves to be left in peace.

segments.text: Hibernation gives children a lovely, gentle idea: that rest is not laziness but survival, and that a sleeping creature deserves to be left in peace.

cards.says: Before you go out. One thing to gather. Identify safe areas to look, log piles, leaf litter, wall cracks. Brief the class: look but do not lift or disturb.

segments.text: Identify safe areas to look, log piles, leaf litter, wall cracks.
Brief the class: look but do not lift or disturb.

cards.says: How it runs. You start with Find a hiding spot. Under logs, in leaf piles, in cracks in walls, under stones. Don't disturb. Just look for likely spots.

segments.text: You start with Find a hiding spot.
Under logs, in leaf piles, in cracks in walls, under stones.

cards.says: Then Feel the shelter. Hibernation spots are chosen carefully. Feel why this spot works: blocked from wind, insulated by leaves.

segments.text: Feel why this spot works: blocked from wind, insulated by leaves.

cards.says: Then Wonder. Kids love this idea. Some will say "amazing." Acknowledge that rest is essential, for animals and for us.

segments.text: Acknowledge that rest is essential, for animals and for us.

cards.says: Then Wish it well. Gentle. Respectful of the sleeping creature. Walk back quietly.

segments.text: Share hiding spots: under logs, leaf piles, walls.

cards.says: Breath. Can you see your own breath?

segments.text: Can you see your own breath?

cards.says: What it is for. In cold air, you can see your own breath, visible proof of being alive. Children watch their warmth meet the cold and discover that their body is a furnace. The skill is noticing by looking.

segments.text: In cold air, you can see your own breath, visible proof of being alive. Children watch their warmth meet the cold and discover that their body is a furnace.
The skill is noticing by looking.

cards.says: The idea to carry. On a cold day you can see your own breath. The warm, damp air from inside your body meets the cold air outside and turns to a little cloud of mist, just for a moment.

segments.text: On a cold day you can see your own breath.
The warm, damp air from inside your body meets the cold air outside and turns to a little cloud of mist, just for a moment.

cards.says: Why it matters. Children are told they are alive, but here they can see it and feel it: warm breath, a warm palm, a body that runs like a little furnace even in the cold.

segments.text: Children are told they are alive, but here they can see it and feel it: warm breath, a warm palm, a body that runs like a little furnace even in the cold.

cards.says: Before you go out. One thing to gather. Best on a cold day when breath is visible. The colder, the better for this practice.

segments.text: Best on a cold day when breath is visible.
The colder, the better for this practice.

cards.says: How it runs. You start with See your breath. Visible breath is winter's gift. You can see yourself being alive. Let them experiment with long slow breaths vs quick puffs.

segments.text: You start with See your breath.

Let them experiment with long slow breaths vs quick puffs.

cards.says: Then Find your breath. Body temperature is remarkable. We generate heat constantly. In winter you can feel the contrast.

segments.text: In winter you can feel the contrast.

cards.says: Then Warm your hands. Generosity of warmth. Touch a cold railing, a frozen bench. You give warmth. Walk back.

segments.text: Touch a cold railing, a frozen bench.

cards.says: And finish in Circle. Simple observation. Joy in visibility. Science connection: metabolism, food as fuel, blood circulation. Generosity metaphor.

segments.text: Science connection: metabolism, food as fuel, blood circulation.

cards.says: Footprints. Who has been here before us?

segments.text: Winter mud and frost reveal who else has been here. Children become detectives: reading tracks, comparing prints, and discovering they share this space with creatures they rarely see.

Birds, dogs, foxes and other animals leave tracks as they pass, and later a child can find them and work out who was here and which way they went.

segments.text: Tracks are proof that children share their space with animals they hardly ever see.
Following that clue builds observation, careful looking, and a kind of gentle detective thinking, working out a story from what was left behind.

Bird feet, dog paws, fox prints if you're lucky.

cards.says: Then Measure a print. Detective work. Reading the ground like a book. Direction, speed, weight.

cards.says: Then Wonder. We share space with creatures we rarely see. The tracks are proof.

cards.says: Then Leave your mark. Adding our mark to the record. Walk back.

segments.text: Adding our mark to the record.

cards.says: What it is for. A practice about water: where it comes from, where it goes, and the extraordinary journey every raindrop has taken. Sensory engagement with puddles, drips, and damp surfaces. The skill is listening and touching.

segments.text: A practice about water: where it comes from, where it goes, and the extraordinary journey every raindrop has taken. Sensory engagement with puddles, drips, and damp surfaces.
The skill is listening and touching.

cards.says: The idea to carry. Every drop of water is a traveller. It falls as rain, soaks into the ground, feeds roots, runs to rivers and the sea, rises into clouds, and falls again.

segments.text: Every drop of water is a traveller.
It falls as rain, soaks into the ground, feeds roots, runs to rivers and the sea, rises into clouds, and falls again.

cards.says: Why it matters. Water is everywhere and easy to ignore. Following its journey gives children a first, wonder-filled grasp of the water cycle and of how everything in nature is connected and reused.

segments.text: Water is everywhere and easy to ignore.
Following its journey gives children a first, wonder-filled grasp of the water cycle and of how everything in nature is connected and reused.

cards.says: Before you go out. One thing to gather. Works best on or just after a rainy day. If dry, look for any standing water, damp surfaces, or dew.

segments.text: Works best on or just after a rainy day.
If dry, look for any standing water, damp surfaces, or dew.

cards.says: How it runs. You start with Find water. Even on dry days there's moisture somewhere. Dew, drainage, damp bark.

segments.text: Even on dry days there's moisture somewhere.

cards.says: Then Touch the water. Let them get their hands wet. Sensory experience matters more than staying clean.

segments.text: Let them get their hands wet.
Sensory experience matters more than staying clean.

cards.says: Then Wonder. A moment of wonder. Some kids will find this mind-blowing.

segments.text: Some kids will find this mind-blowing.

cards.says: Then Thank the rain. Simple. Walk back.
And finish in Circle. Puddles, leaves, bark, soil. Follow the journey: ground, roots, river, sea, cloud. Connects to ecology and care.

segments.text: Follow the journey: ground, roots, river, sea, cloud.

cards.says: Green. How many different greens can you find?

segments.text: How many different greens can you find?

cards.says: What it is for. A perception exercise. Children discover that green is not one colour but dozens: dark moss, bright leaf, pale lichen, emerald grass. Then they name their favourite with a feeling-word. The skill is looking.

segments.text: A perception exercise. Children discover that green is not one colour but dozens: dark moss, bright leaf, pale lichen, emerald grass. Then they name their favourite with a feeling-word.

cards.says: The idea to carry. We call it all green, but green is really dozens of different shades: dark moss, bright new leaf, pale lichen, deep emerald grass. This is a perception practice.

segments.text: We call it all green, but green is really dozens of different shades: dark moss, bright new leaf, pale lichen, deep emerald grass.

cards.says: Why it matters. Looking closely is a skill, and most children glance rather than see. Discovering that a single colour holds many shades sharpens attention and delights them.

segments.text: Looking closely is a skill, and most children glance rather than see.
Discovering that a single colour holds many shades sharpens attention and delights them.

cards.says: Before you go out. One thing to gather. No preparation. Works anywhere there is vegetation, even a single tree or patch of grass.

segments.text: Works anywhere there is vegetation, even a single tree or patch of grass.

cards.says: How it runs. You start with Spot a new green. This is a perception exercise. Most kids will say 3-4, then start finding 10, 15, 20 variations.

segments.text: You start with Spot a new green.
Most kids will say 3-4, then start finding 10, 15, 20 variations.

cards.says: Then Stand with your green. Let them choose. No wrong answer. Dark moss, bright leaf, pale lichen.

segments.text: Dark moss, bright leaf, pale lichen.

cards.says: Then Wonder. Colour preference reveals something personal. Light touch.
Then Name your green. Calm green. Electric green. Sleepy green. Let them be creative.
And finish in Circle. Compare numbers. Usually way more than expected. Share the creative names. Celebrate imagination. Connects to biodiversity, light, seasons.

segments.text: Each has a plain definition and a child's version, already written.

cards.says: Seeds. What could one small seed become?

segments.text: What could one small seed become?

cards.says: What it is for. Children find and hold seeds: dandelion fluff, acorns, berries, grass seeds. Each one contains a whole future. A practice about potential and careful attention. The skill is touching and looking.

segments.text: Children find and hold seeds: dandelion fluff, acorns, berries, grass seeds. Each one contains a whole future. A practice about potential and careful attention.
The skill is touching and looking.

cards.says: The idea to carry. A seed is a small, quiet package with a whole plant folded inside it, waiting. Dandelion fluff, acorns, grass seeds, the pips in a berry: each one carries the next generation.

segments.text: A seed is a small, quiet package with a whole plant folded inside it, waiting.
Dandelion fluff, acorns, grass seeds, the pips in a berry: each one carries the next generation.

cards.says: Why it matters. Seeds are a gentle way into big ideas: potential, patience, and the future hidden inside small things. Holding an acorn and picturing an oak stretches a child's imagination and their sense of time.

segments.text: Seeds are a gentle way into big ideas: potential, patience, and the future hidden inside small things.
Holding an acorn and picturing an oak stretches a child's imagination and their sense of time.

cards.says: Before you go out. One thing to gather. Best in an area with seed-bearing plants, dandelions, grasses, trees with fallen seeds or acorns.

segments.text: Best in an area with seed-bearing plants, dandelions, grasses, trees with fallen seeds or acorns.

cards.says: How it runs. You start with Find a seed. Dandelion seeds, acorns, berries, grass seeds. Anything that carries the next generation.

segments.text: You start with Find a seed.
Dandelion seeds, acorns, berries, grass seeds.
Anything that carries the next generation.

cards.says: Then Hold it. Weight, texture, shape. A whole tree fits in an acorn.

segments.text: A whole tree fits in an acorn.

cards.says: Then Wonder. Metaphor territory. Some kids will get it, some won't. Both fine.

segments.text: Some kids will get it, some won't.

cards.says: Then Put it back. Place it gently. Don't throw. Walk back.
And finish in Circle. Describe it: size, colour, where it was. A tree, a flower, food for something. Optional. Beautiful question for the right class.

segments.text: Describe it: size, colour, where it was.
A tree, a flower, food for something.
Beautiful question for the right class.

cards.says: Gratitude walk. Finding three living things to thank.

segments.text: Finding three living things to thank.

cards.says: What it is for. The closing practice of spring. Children walk slowly, choose three living things, and thank them by name. A practice in gratitude, attention, and speaking kindness aloud. The skill is feeling and looking.

segments.text: The closing practice of spring. Children walk slowly, choose three living things, and thank them by name. A practice in gratitude, attention, and speaking kindness aloud.
The skill is feeling and looking.

cards.says: The idea to carry. This is the closing practice of spring. Children walk slowly, choose three living things they want to thank, stand with each one, and say its name and thank you, out loud.

segments.text: This is the closing practice of spring.
Children walk slowly, choose three living things they want to thank, stand with each one, and say its name and thank you, out loud.

cards.says: Why it matters. Saying thank you out loud to a living thing feels strange at first and then quietly powerful. Gratitude, spoken and specific, deepens the bond children have been building with the outdoors all term.

segments.text: Saying thank you out loud to a living thing feels strange at first and then quietly powerful.
Gratitude, spoken and specific, deepens the bond children have been building with the outdoors all term.

cards.says: Before you go out. One thing to gather. No preparation. This works in any outdoor space where living things can be found.

segments.text: This works in any outdoor space where living things can be found.

cards.says: How it runs. You start with Find three living things. Tree, flower, bird, insect, grass, moss. Anything alive. Three is enough.

segments.text: You start with Find three living things.
Tree, flower, bird, insect, grass, moss.

cards.says: Then Stand with each one. Slow looking. 30 seconds per thing. Notice detail.
Then Wonder. It could be beauty, shade, oxygen, food, sound. Personal reasons.

segments.text: It could be beauty, shade, oxygen, food, sound.

cards.says: Then Say thank you. Thank you, oak tree. Thank you, robin. Thank you, moss. Model this first. It will feel awkward and then wonderful.

segments.text: It will feel awkward and then wonderful.

cards.says: And finish in Circle. Go around the circle. Every answer is valid. Often the gratitude that surprises us is the most real. Close the season with this. Let them sit with the feeling.

segments.text: Often the gratitude that surprises us is the most real.
Let them sit with the feeling.

cards.says: Four words to have ready. Each has a plain definition and a child's version, already written.

segments.text: Each has a plain definition and a child's version, already written.

cards.says: Counting life. What's living in our grounds?
What it is for. Notice everything that is alive around you and begin to work out what it means to be living - breathing, growing, reproducing, dying. The skill is looking and listening.

segments.text: Notice everything that is alive around you and begin to work out what it means to be living - breathing, growing, reproducing, dying.
The skill is looking and listening.

cards.says: The idea to carry. Children count everything alive within ten steps of where they stand, then begin to work out what makes something living: breathing, growing, reproducing, dying.

segments.text: Children count everything alive within ten steps of where they stand, then begin to work out what makes something living: breathing, growing, reproducing, dying.

cards.says: Why it matters. Naming what is alive is the first step to caring about it. A child who has counted dozens of living things in one corner of the playground never sees "nothing" there again.

segments.text: Naming what is alive is the first step to caring about it.
A child who has counted dozens of living things in one corner of the playground never sees "nothing" there again.

cards.says: Before you go out. Nothing to bring. Walk out as you are.
How it runs. You start with Count. Set the boundary first: ten steps from where you stand, no further. Pairs work well.

segments.text: Set the boundary first: ten steps from where you stand, no further.

cards.says: Then See. Encourage children to look up, down, under...

segments.text: Encourage children to look up, down, under...

cards.says: Then Hear. Try thirty seconds of complete silence first. The longer the quiet, the more they hear.

segments.text: Try thirty seconds of complete silence first.
The longer the quiet, the more they hear.

cards.says: Then Alive. Let them argue. A fallen leaf, a seed, moss on a wall: alive or not? The wondering is the learning.

segments.text: A fallen leaf, a seed, moss on a wall: alive or not?

cards.says: Then Living. Four signs they can test anything against. Try them on a bird, a tree, a stone.

segments.text: Four signs they can test anything against.
Try them on a bird, a tree, a stone.

cards.says: And finish in Circle. Let a few children share with the whole circle. A feather, a seed, a fallen leaf. Hard cases make the best thinking. No right answer. Big guesses welcome.

segments.text: Let a few children share with the whole circle.
A feather, a seed, a fallen leaf.
Hard cases make the best thinking.

cards.says: Minibeast hunting.
What it is for. Look closely at minibeasts and discover that all creatures have special roles to help our planet stay alive. The skill is looking and touching.

segments.text: Look closely at minibeasts and discover that all creatures have special roles to help our planet stay alive.
The skill is looking and touching.

cards.says: The idea to carry. Children hunt for minibeasts in soil, under logs and in bushes, look closely at legs, wings and homes, and learn that every creature has a special role.

segments.text: Children hunt for minibeasts in soil, under logs and in bushes, look closely at legs, wings and homes, and learn that every creature has a special role.

cards.says: Why it matters. Minibeasts are the easiest wild animals for children to meet up close. Handling them gently is a first lesson in respect for living things: gentle hands, quiet voices, and everything goes back exactly where it was found.

segments.text: Minibeasts are the easiest wild animals for children to meet up close.
Handling them gently is a first lesson in respect for living things: gentle hands, quiet voices, and everything goes back exactly where it was found.

cards.says: Before you go out. Two things to gather. Bring the bug pots or viewers and magnifying glasses. If you can, check your patch the day before: lift a log, see who is home.

segments.text: Bring the bug pots or viewers and magnifying glasses.
If you can, check your patch the day before: lift a log, see who is home.

cards.says: How it runs. You start with Settle. Give this longer than feels comfortable. A class goes quiet on its own once it is hunting for a sound, and the quiet you wait for lasts longer than the quiet you ask for. Say this one clearly.

segments.text: Give this longer than feels comfortable.
A class goes quiet on its own once it is hunting for a sound, and the quiet you wait for lasts longer than the quiet you ask for.

cards.says: Then Engage. Allow children to raise their hands to give feedback.

segments.text: Allow children to raise their hands to give feedback.

cards.says: Then Explore. Give children 10 minutes to explore their outdoor space, using only their senses.

segments.text: Give children 10 minutes to explore their outdoor space, using only their senses.

cards.says: Then Identify. Bring the class back to the circle. Let them discuss in partners or raise their hands.

segments.text: Bring the class back to the circle.
Let them discuss in partners or raise their hands.

cards.says: Then Appreciate. Allow your class to go back to a spot in your grounds to thank the minibeasts.

segments.text: Allow your class to go back to a spot in your grounds to thank the minibeasts.

cards.says: And finish in Circle. We borrow, we look, we give back. The whole lesson in one move. Any guess counts as thinking like a scientist.

segments.text: We borrow, we look, we give back.
The whole lesson in one move.
Any guess counts as thinking like a scientist.

cards.says: A5 leaf collage.
What it is for. Create art with nature, taking influence from what the children see around them. The skill is touching and looking.

segments.text: Create art with nature, taking influence from what the children see around them.
The skill is touching and looking.

cards.says: The idea to carry. Children collect leaves outside and glue them into patterns and pictures on A5 paper, taking influence from what they can see around them.

segments.text: Children collect leaves outside and glue them into patterns and pictures on A5 paper, taking influence from what they can see around them.

cards.says: Why it matters. Making art with found nature asks children to look twice: once at the leaf, once at the world. The picture is theirs; the materials belong to the place.

segments.text: Making art with found nature asks children to look twice: once at the leaf, once at the world.
The picture is theirs; the materials belong to the place.

cards.says: Before you go out. Three things to gather. Glue sticks and A5 paper in a bag. One sheet per child, plus a few spares.

segments.text: Glue sticks and A5 paper in a bag.
One sheet per child, plus a few spares.

cards.says: How it runs. You start with Collect. Ask children to gather fallen leaves and petals from the ground — ones that have already fallen.

segments.text: Ask children to gather fallen leaves and petals from the ground — ones that have already fallen.

cards.says: Then Create. Gather the children back inside. Let them take their time with this.

segments.text: Let them take their time with this.

cards.says: Then Glue. Give the class ideas, drawing on what they saw in nature.

segments.text: Give the class ideas, drawing on what they saw in nature.

cards.says: Then Present. Ask if anyone wants to show their art to the rest of the class.

segments.text: Ask if anyone wants to show their art to the rest of the class.

cards.says: And finish in Circle. Shape, colour, size, smell. Descriptive language lives here. Back to the earth. Nothing in nature is wasted.
Our Earth's magnificent trees. Why are trees so important for our existence?

segments.text: Why are trees so important for our existence?

cards.says: What it is for. Understand why trees matter for our existence (humans) and for the other creatures on our planet. The skill is looking and touching.

segments.text: Understand why trees matter for our existence (humans) and for the other creatures on our planet.
The skill is looking and touching.

cards.says: The idea to carry. Children walk among the trees of their outside space and talk about why trees matter: for the air we breathe and for the creatures that live in and around them.

segments.text: Children walk among the trees of their outside space and talk about why trees matter: for the air we breathe and for the creatures that live in and around them.

cards.says: Why it matters. A child who has thanked a tree treats trees differently. This session turns the biggest living things on the school grounds from scenery into neighbours.

segments.text: A child who has thanked a tree treats trees differently.
This session turns the biggest living things on the school grounds from scenery into neighbours.

cards.says: Before you go out. Nothing to bring.

How it runs. You start with Settle. Give this longer than feels comfortable. A class goes quiet on its own once it is hunting for a sound, and the quiet you wait for lasts longer than the quiet you ask for. Say this one clearly.

segments.text: Give this longer than feels comfortable.
A class goes quiet on its own once it is hunting for a sound, and the quiet you wait for lasts longer than the quiet you ask for.

cards.says: Then Walk. Bark, leaves, height, shape. How many different trees can the class spot?

segments.text: How many different trees can the class spot?

cards.says: Then Discuss. Prompt children to discuss amongst themselves. They produce the air we need to breathe (oxygen).

segments.text: Prompt children to discuss amongst themselves.
They produce the air we need to breathe (oxygen).

cards.says: Then Creatures. e.g. birds for homes and food (nuts and fruit), insects.

segments.text: e.g. birds for homes and food (nuts and fruit), insects.

cards.says: Then Imagine. Sit with the question. Let the silence do some of the teaching.

segments.text: Let the silence do some of the teaching.

cards.says: And finish in Circle. Some children will whisper it to themselves. That counts.

segments.text: Some children will whisper it to themselves.

cards.says: Warmth. What has the sun been warming?

segments.text: What has the sun been warming?

cards.says: What it is for. Children explore where the sun is touching: their bodies, surfaces, the ground. A practice about solar energy, warmth as nourishment, and the 93-million-mile journey of light. The skill is touching and looking.

segments.text: Children explore where the sun is touching: their bodies, surfaces, the ground. A practice about solar energy, warmth as nourishment, and the 93-million-mile journey of light.
The skill is touching and looking.

cards.says: The idea to carry. The sun warms us directly, on our skin, and it warms the things around us: walls, stones, soil, bark. Some surfaces hold that heat and stay warm long after the sun has moved.

segments.text: The sun warms us directly, on our skin, and it warms the things around us: walls, stones, soil, bark.
Some surfaces hold that heat and stay warm long after the sun has moved.

cards.says: Why it matters. The warmth children feel outside is the same energy that grows every plant and feeds every food chain. Starting summer by noticing it turns a hot day from something to complain about into something to be grateful for.

segments.text: The warmth children feel outside is the same energy that grows every plant and feeds every food chain.
Starting summer by noticing it turns a hot day from something to complain about into something to be grateful for.

cards.says: Before you go out. One thing to gather. Best on a sunny day. If overcast, focus on warm surfaces and sheltered spots.

segments.text: If overcast, focus on warm surfaces and sheltered spots.

cards.says: How it runs. You start with Feel the sun. Face, arms, top of head. Let them notice the warmth: which side is lit, which is in shadow.

segments.text: You start with Feel the sun.
Let them notice the warmth: which side is lit, which is in shadow.

cards.says: Then Find the warm thing. A wall, a stone, a fence post, dark bark. Compare warm surfaces to cool shaded ones.

segments.text: A wall, a stone, a fence post, dark bark.
Compare warm surfaces to cool shaded ones.

cards.says: Then Wonder. This connects warmth to nourishment. Kids might say "nice" or "relaxed". All good.
Then Thank the sun. 93 million miles. You can mention that if you want. Kids love the number.

segments.text: You can mention that if you want.

cards.says: And finish in Circle. Compare surfaces: stone, metal, wood, soil. Shadow, under a tree, near water. Opens up ecology, food chains, gratitude.

segments.text: Compare surfaces: stone, metal, wood, soil.
Shadow, under a tree, near water.
Opens up ecology, food chains, gratitude.

segments.text: Each has a plain definition and a child's version, already written.

cards.says: The pollinators. Follow one flyer and watch it work.

segments.text: Follow one flyer and watch it work.

cards.says: What it is for. A patient observation practice. Children find a flying insect (a bee, butterfly, or hoverfly) and follow it slowly, watching it work from flower to flower. The skill is looking and listening.

segments.text: A patient observation practice. Children find a flying insect (a bee, butterfly, or hoverfly) and follow it slowly, watching it work from flower to flower.
The skill is looking and listening.

cards.says: The idea to carry. Children find a flying insect, a bee, a butterfly, or a hoverfly, and follow it slowly as it moves from flower to flower. Without ever needing the word pollination, they watch it happen.

segments.text: Children find a flying insect, a bee, a butterfly, or a hoverfly, and follow it slowly as it moves from flower to flower.
Without ever needing the word pollination, they watch it happen.

cards.says: Why it matters. Pollinators carry pollen between flowers so plants can make seeds and fruit. A great deal of the food we eat depends on them.

segments.text: Pollinators carry pollen between flowers so plants can make seeds and fruit.
A great deal of the food we eat depends on them.

cards.says: Before you go out. One thing to gather. Best near flowering plants on a warm day when insects are active. Scout for bee-friendly areas.

segments.text: Best near flowering plants on a warm day when insects are active.

cards.says: How it runs. You start with Find a flyer. Sit or stand near flowers. Be patient. Movement will come.

segments.text: You start with Find a flyer.

cards.says: Then Follow a flyer. This is a meditation in patience. Some kids will want to catch things. Redirect: "We're following, not catching."

segments.text: This is a meditation in patience.
Some kids will want to catch things.

cards.says: Then Wonder. Pollination without the textbook. They're witnessing it happen.
Then Thank the workers. Whisper it. Bees don't care, but the children will remember saying it.

segments.text: Bees don't care, but the children will remember saying it.

cards.says: And finish in Circle. Let them tell the story of their pollinator's journey. Count if they can. The number often surprises them. Connects to food systems. Powerful for older KS2.

segments.text: Let them tell the story of their pollinator's journey.

cards.says: Four words to have ready. Each has a plain definition and a child's version, already written.

segments.text: Each has a plain definition and a child's version, already written.

cards.says: Shade. Where is the coolest place, and what made it?

segments.text: Where is the coolest place, and what made it?

cards.says: What it is for. Children seek out the coolest spots and discover microclimates: how a tree creates shelter, how soil holds moisture, how shade is a gift from something alive. The skill is touching and listening.

segments.text: Children seek out the coolest spots and discover microclimates: how a tree creates shelter, how soil holds moisture, how shade is a gift from something alive.
The skill is touching and listening.

cards.says: The idea to carry. On a warm day, some places stay cool: under a tree, against a shaded wall, in long grass, near water.

segments.text: On a warm day, some places stay cool: under a tree, against a shaded wall, in long grass, near water.

cards.says: Why it matters. Shade is easy to take for granted until a hot day. Noticing that a living tree creates shelter, and that soil and stone hold coolness, helps children see the outdoors as something that looks after them.

segments.text: Shade is easy to take for granted until a hot day.
Noticing that a living tree creates shelter, and that soil and stone hold coolness, helps children see the outdoors as something that looks after them.

cards.says: Before you go out. One thing to gather. Best on a warm day when the contrast between sun and shade is noticeable.

segments.text: Best on a warm day when the contrast between sun and shade is noticeable.

cards.says: How it runs. You start with Find the coolest spot. Under a tree, against a north-facing wall, near water, in long grass. Let them explore.

segments.text: You start with Find the coolest spot.
Under a tree, against a north-facing wall, near water, in long grass.

cards.says: Then Sit in the cool. A tree made shade. Soil holds moisture. Stone stays cool. They're discovering microclimates.
Then Wonder. The tree didn't mean to shelter you, but it does. That's a gift.

segments.text: The tree didn't mean to shelter you, but it does.

cards.says: Then Thank the shade. A hand on the trunk. A pat on the grass. Walk back together.
And finish in Circle. Compare spots. Why was one cooler than another? Trees, buildings, walls: nature vs human-made. Animals, insects, plants. Shade is shared.

segments.text: Why was one cooler than another?
Trees, buildings, walls: nature vs human-made.

segments.text: Each has a plain definition and a child's version, already written.

cards.says: Smell. What is the strongest smell you can find?

segments.text: What is the strongest smell you can find?

cards.says: What it is for. Summer has the strongest scents. Children explore smell as the most memory-linked sense: crushing leaves, sniffing bark, getting close to flowers. The skill is smelling and touching.

segments.text: Summer has the strongest scents. Children explore smell as the most memory-linked sense: crushing leaves, sniffing bark, getting close to flowers.
The skill is smelling and touching.

cards.says: The idea to carry. Warm air carries scent, so summer is the richest season for smells: cut grass, warm soil, flowers, herbs, rain on hot ground.

segments.text: Warm air carries scent, so summer is the richest season for smells: cut grass, warm soil, flowers, herbs, rain on hot ground.

cards.says: Why it matters. Smell is the sense we teach children the least, yet it is the one most tied to memory and feeling.

segments.text: Smell is the sense we teach children the least, yet it is the one most tied to memory and feeling.

cards.says: Before you go out. One thing to gather. No preparation. Summer produces strong natural scents everywhere.

segments.text: Summer produces strong natural scents everywhere.

cards.says: How it runs. You start with Notice the smells. Cut grass, warm soil, flowers, rain, hot tarmac. Summer has the strongest smells.

segments.text: You start with Notice the smells.
Cut grass, warm soil, flowers, rain, hot tarmac.

cards.says: Then Chase a smell. Crush a leaf gently between fingers. Sniff bark. Get close to flowers. Hands-on smelling.

segments.text: Crush a leaf gently between fingers.

cards.says: Then Wonder. Smell triggers memory more than any other sense. Let them share if they want to.

segments.text: Smell triggers memory more than any other sense.
Let them share if they want to.

cards.says: Then Keep the scent. Anchoring the memory. Walk back breathing slowly.
And finish in Circle. Encourage specific, descriptive language. Smell-memory connection. Often surprising stories emerge. Connects seasons, anticipation.

cards.says: Food. What has already been eaten here?

segments.text: What has already been eaten here?

cards.says: What it is for. Everything is food for something. Children find evidence of feeding (nibbled leaves, pecked fruit, nectar being collected) and discover their schoolyard is a living food web. The skill is looking and touching.

segments.text: Everything is food for something. Children find evidence of feeding (nibbled leaves, pecked fruit, nectar being collected) and discover their schoolyard is a living food web.
The skill is looking and touching.

cards.says: The idea to carry. Everything outside is food for something. Leaves feed caterpillars, seeds feed birds, nectar feeds bees, berries feed many creatures at once. Rather than watching the eating happen, children look for the evidence of it: holes in leaves, nibbled edges, pecked fruit.

segments.text: Everything outside is food for something.

cards.says: Flowers. What can you see inside a flower?

segments.text: What can you see inside a flower?

cards.says: What it is for. Flowers compete for attention. Children find the loudest colour, look inside a flower, and discover the hidden world of pollen, patterns, and tiny structures. The skill is looking and smelling.

segments.text: Flowers compete for attention. Children find the loudest colour, look inside a flower, and discover the hidden world of pollen, patterns, and tiny structures.

segments.text: Their colour is an advertisement, calling pollinators in to feed.

cards.says: Long day. Where will the sun set tonight?

segments.text: Where will the sun set tonight?

cards.says: What it is for. Summer days are the longest. Children trace the sun's arc, play with shadows, and reflect on what long light means for the land and for themselves. The skill is noticing by looking.

segments.text: Summer days are the longest. Children trace the sun's arc, play with shadows, and reflect on what long light means for the land and for themselves.

cards.says: The idea to carry. Children point to where the sun is now and where it will set, hunt for the longest and shortest shadows, and notice how late the summer light lasts.

segments.text: Children point to where the sun is now and where it will set, hunt for the longest and shortest shadows, and notice how late the summer light lasts.

segments.text: The Earth is tilted as it travels round the sun, and in summer our half of the world leans towards it, giving long days and short nights.

cards.says: Before you go out. One thing to gather. Best on a sunny day. Note which direction is west (sunset) before going out.

segments.text: Note which direction is west (sunset) before going out.

cards.says: Then Wonder. Joy, energy, not wanting to go to bed. All valid. This connects to seasonal rhythms.

segments.text: The final summer practice. Children count everything alive within arm's reach and discover they are standing in a crowd of living things. A practice about noticing how much life surrounds us.

cards.says: Then Thank them all. Close the summer season. A collective thank you. Walk back together slowly.

cards.says: What it is for. Design and build a simple bird feeder using a recycled plastic bottle. The skill is designing and making.

cards.says: The idea to carry. Children sketch a design for a bird feeder, then build a simple version from a recycled plastic bottle, before taking it outside to hang it on site. Indoors first: what birds struggle to find in winter, and how we could help.

segments.text: Explore the different textures and patterns of tree bark using a simple rubbing technique.

cards.says: The idea to carry. Children use paper and crayons to take rubbings from different tree trunks around the school grounds, then compare the patterns. Indoors first: what does bark feel like, is every tree's the same, and how a rubbing works.

cards.says: What it is for. Survey one patch of the grounds and describe how it provides for the basic needs of the animals and plants living in it, and how one living thing there depends on another. The skill is surveying and describing.

segments.text: Survey one patch of the grounds and describe how it provides for the basic needs of the animals and plants living in it, and how one living thing there depends on another.
The skill is surveying and describing.

cards.says: The idea to carry. Children sort their list of needs into two: animals need air, water and food, and most need shelter; plants need light, air and water, and somewhere to grow.

segments.text: Children sort their list of needs into two: animals need air, water and food, and most need shelter; plants need light, air and water, and somewhere to grow.

cards.says: Why it matters. The statutory bullet asks for two things at once: that a habitat suits what lives in it, and that the things living in it depend on each other.

segments.text: The statutory bullet asks for two things at once: that a habitat suits what lives in it, and that the things living in it depend on each other.

cards.says: Before you go out. Three things to gather. Choose four or five patches around the grounds that are honestly different from each other: mown grass, under a hedge, a wall foot, a border, a puddle edge. Different is the point, not pretty.

segments.text: Choose four or five patches around the grounds that are honestly different from each other: mown grass, under a hedge, a wall foot, a border, a puddle edge.
Different is the point, not pretty.

cards.says: How it runs. You start with Settle. Give this longer than feels comfortable. A class goes quiet on its own once it is hunting for a sound, and the quiet you wait for lasts longer than the quiet you ask for. Say this one clearly.

segments.text: Give this longer than feels comfortable.
A class goes quiet on its own once it is hunting for a sound, and the quiet you wait for lasts longer than the quiet you ask for.

cards.says: Then Introduce. Take every answer, then sort the list with them into two columns: what animals need and what plants need. Animals need air, water and food, and most need shelter. Plants need light, air and water, and somewhere to grow.

segments.text: Take every answer, then sort the list with them into two columns: what animals need and what plants need.
Animals need air, water and food, and most need shelter.
Plants need light, air and water, and somewhere to grow.

cards.says: Then Survey your patch. This is the honesty the whole unit rests on. A patch that gives some of what is needed and not the rest is a good finding, and a class that invents the missing ones has learnt to make things up.

segments.text: This is the honesty the whole unit rests on.
A patch that gives some of what is needed and not the rest is a good finding, and a class that invents the missing ones has learnt to make things up.

cards.says: Then Who needs whom. A caterpillar and the leaf it is eating. A hedge and a bird nesting in it. Both halves must be living, so a stone does not count.

segments.text: A caterpillar and the leaf it is eating.
A hedge and a bird nesting in it.
Both halves must be living, so a stone does not count.

cards.says: And finish in Circle time. Nearest is the useful word here. A patch with no water is fine if a puddle is a hop away, and that is what a home range means without the phrase.

segments.text: Nearest is the useful word here.
A patch with no water is fine if a puddle is a hop away, and that is what a home range means without the phrase.

cards.says: Three words to have ready. Each has a plain definition and a child's version, already written.

cards.says: Simple food chains. Where does the food in our grounds begin?

segments.text: Where does the food in our grounds begin?

cards.says: What it is for. Build a simple food chain from living things found in the grounds, naming each link the class has seen and leaving a question on each link it has not. The skill is linking and explaining.

segments.text: Build a simple food chain from living things found in the grounds, naming each link the class has seen and leaving a question on each link it has not.
The skill is linking and explaining.

cards.says: The idea to carry. Children meet the words for who eats what, then go out and find the bottom of a chain: a plant, and something that is eating it.

segments.text: Children meet the words for who eats what, then go out and find the bottom of a chain: a plant, and something that is eating it.

cards.says: Why it matters. The arrow is the idea, and it goes the way a book does not: it points at the eater, because the arrow shows where the food goes.

segments.text: The arrow is the idea, and it goes the way a book does not: it points at the eater, because the arrow shows where the food goes.

cards.says: Before you go out. Four things to gather. Cut three strips of card for each pair, big enough to draw on. If your class kept its sheets from the earlier lessons, put them out: the chain is built from what they already found.

cards.says: Then Introduce. Three words on the board. Ask which one they are, and take the argument that follows: most of the class will be omnivores and will want to say carnivore.

cards.says: Then Find the bottom of a chain. Chewed edges and holes suggest an eater but not which one. Unless a child has watched a creature eating that plant, the second strip stays blank with the question on it.

cards.says: Then Build the chain. Build the chain from what this class actually found, not out of a book.

cards.says: And finish in Circle time. One meal is not a whole diet, so do not call a link herbivore or carnivore from its place in the chain. Predator and prey only apply where somebody saw one animal eat another.
